summary:
Ontario stands under the framework of Canada. The Ontario Human Rights Code expressly prohibits discrimination and harassment on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The Ontario Human Rights Commission's published policy on gender identity and gender expression is the official provincial statement of these protections, defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender, and notes that a chosen name and a pronoun are common ways of expressing gender.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, 1% more than in 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate, at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population. This ranking is by raw rate as published; police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting levels are shaped by awareness and community trust. Egale Canada, an LGBTIQ+ organisation, published a 2024 hate-crime analysis of national police-reported data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations.

Ontario did not adopt parental-consent legislation on school names and pronouns. On 28 August 2023, Ontario education minister Stephen Lecce said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school, speaking the same week Saskatchewan joined New Brunswick in legislating parental consent for students under 16; he said teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-provincial policy turbulence in Canada is concentrated in schools and sport and sits outside Ontario: Saskatchewan's 2023 Education (Parents' Bill of Rights) Amendment Act invoked the notwithstanding clause to require parental consent for students under 16 who ask to use a gender-related preferred name or their gender identity, drawing calls for repeal and litigation; Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, the Education Amendment Act and the Fairness and Safety in Sport Act in 2024, then shielded them through Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, 2025, again using the notwithstanding clause.

As of 2017, all federal, provincial and territorial human rights acts explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, including in employment, housing and public and private accommodations. Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms has been interpreted so that the concepts of sex and physical disability include transsexuality, providing equal-protection guidance for courts interpreting human rights laws. Transgender people are able to change their legal gender in all provinces and territories under varying rules.

A Privy Council Office poll reported for 2020 found 87.6% said they would be 'comfortable' if a neighbour was a transgender person, while 91.8% said the same of a next-door neighbour who was gay, lesbian or bisexual, a gap indicating lower comfort with transgender neighbours than with sexual-minority neighbours.
localsOnly:
Ontario residents are covered by the Ontario Human Rights Code's gender identity and gender expression protections across employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations, with the Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy setting out the legislation, case law and complaint route.

Ontario schools operate without a parental-consent statute on names and pronouns; the education minister's August 2023 position was that parents must be fully involved and aware, with teachers and school boards weighing exceptional circumstances and potential harm to the child.

Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate of police-reported hate crime in 2024, at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population, above the national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. The figure covers all reported motivations, not only anti-LGBTQ+ incidents, and reflects only incidents reported to and recorded by police.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Statistics Canada release breaks out motivations in categories that do not establish trans-specific hate-crime volume in Ontario; Egale Canada's analysis covers both sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations nationally, but no Ontario-specific gender-identity breakdown is sourced here.

Whether Ontario has since adopted any parental-consent or school-notice measure after the minister's August 2023 statement is unresolved in this inventory; the sources establish only that no such legislation had been adopted at that time.
